claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease affecting the elderly worldwide.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease affecting the elderly worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about AD prevalence.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been proposed as a key event in the etiology of AD.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been proposed as a key event in the etiology of AD.
evidence: This refers to existing scientific literature and hypotheses about AD etiology.

claim: GRU102 is a transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans strain expressing human Aβ peptide specifically in neurons.
source: We have previously modeled amyloid-beta (Aβ)-induced mitochondrial dysfunction in a transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans strain by expressing human Aβ peptide specifically in neurons (GRU102).
evidence: This describes the experimental model created and characterized by the authors.

claim: GRU102 showed reduced activity of alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
source: In particular, GRU102 showed reduced activity of a rate-limiting TCA cycle enzyme, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Metabolic failure occurred before any significant increase in global protein aggregate was detectable in GRU102.
source: Importantly, metabolic failure occurred before any significant increase in global protein aggregate was detectable.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of metabolic and aggregation data in the manuscript.

claim: Metformin treatment reversed Aβ-induced metabolic defects in GRU102.
source: Treatment with an anti-diabetes drug, Metformin, reversed Aβ-induced metabolic defects, reduced protein aggregation and normalized lifespan of GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Metformin treatment studies.

claim: Metformin treatment reduced protein aggregation in GRU102.
source: Treatment with an anti-diabetes drug, Metformin, reversed Aβ-induced metabolic defects, reduced protein aggregation and normalized lifespan of GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by protein aggregation assay data from Metformin-treated animals.

claim: Metformin treatment normalized lifespan of GRU102.
source: Treatment with an anti-diabetes drug, Metformin, reversed Aβ-induced metabolic defects, reduced protein aggregation and normalized lifespan of GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction is an early and causative event in Aβ-induced pathology.
source: Our results point to metabolic dysfunction as an early and causative event in Aβ-induced pathology and a promising target for intervention.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal sequence of events observed in the study.

claim: AD is clinically characterized by the formation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein in the brain.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disease, that is clinically characterized by the formation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein in the brain (Mirra et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on AD pathology.

claim: Perturbations in mitochondrial functions including energy metabolism have been observed in the brain of AD subjects.
source: Even though AD is primarily a neuronal disorder, perturbations in mitochondrial functions including energy metabolism have consistently been observed not only in the brain (Gibson et al., 1998; Gibson et al., 1999; Müller et al., 2010) but also in non-neuronal cells derived from AD subjects, including in fibroblasts and platelets (Bosetti et al., 2002; Blass and Gibson, 1992; Cardoso et al., 2004; Curti et al., 1997; Parker et al., 1994; Swerdlow, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Perturbations in mitochondrial functions have been observed in non-neuronal cells derived from AD subjects, including in fibroblasts and platelets.
source: Even though AD is primarily a neuronal disorder, perturbations in mitochondrial functions including energy metabolism have consistently been observed not only in the brain (Gibson et al., 1998; Gibson et al., 1999; Müller et al., 2010) but also in non-neuronal cells derived from AD subjects, including in fibroblasts and platelets (Bosetti et al., 2002; Blass and Gibson, 1992; Cardoso et al., 2004; Curti et al., 1997; Parker et al., 1994; Swerdlow, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Metabolic defects may precede Aβ aggregate formation in AD.
source: These findings form part of an emerging story that there is an important metabolic component to the etiology of AD (de la Monte and Wands, 2008), and that these metabolic defects may precede Aβ aggregate formation (Yao et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research suggesting temporal sequence.

claim: AD is, in part, mediated by impairments to the brain's insulin response, which promotes oxidative stress and inflammation, similar to that of diabetes.
source: The metabolism-related hypothesis of AD therefore posits that AD is, in part, mediated by impairments to the brain's insulin response, which promotes oxidative stress and inflammation, similar to that of diabetes (de la Monte and Wands, 2008; McClean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intranasal insulin treatment has been shown to ameliorate AD pathology in a transgenic rat model.
source: Moreover, intranasal insulin treatment has been shown to ameliorate AD pathology in a transgenic rat model and to improve mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in patients (Craft et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2016; Craft et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Intranasal insulin treatment has been shown to improve mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in patients.
source: Moreover, intranasal insulin treatment has been shown to ameliorate AD pathology in a transgenic rat model and to improve mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in patients (Craft et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2016; Craft et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Energy deficits, reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential, abnormal mitochondrial gene expression and increased oxidative stress have been observed early in transgenic AD mice (2–3 months of age) well before the appearance of Aβ plaques.
source: Energy deficits, reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential, abnormal mitochondrial gene expression and increased oxidative stress have been observed early in transgenic AD mice (2–3 months of age) well before the appearance of Aβ plaques (Reddy et al., 2004; Hauptmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: Aβ, predominantly its oligomeric form, can directly induce oxidative stress by inserting itself into the lipid bilayer, subsequently leading to lipid peroxidation and protein oxidation.
source: The Aβ-induced oxidative stress hypothesis further posits that Aβ, predominantly its oligomeric form, can directly induce oxidative stress by inserting itself into the lipid bilayer, subsequently leading to lipid peroxidation and protein oxidation (Swomley and Butterfield, 2015; Swomley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Oxidative modification to specific enzymes involved in glucose metabolism has been confirmed in brain of AD and MCI patients.
source: Oxidative modification to specific enzymes involved in glucose metabolism has also been confirmed in brain of AD and MCI patients (Butterfield et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2009), further supporting the hypothesis that Aβ-induced oxidative stress contributes to defects in metabolism, impairs glucose metabolism, before leading to synaptic dysfunction and ultimately neuronal death in AD (Butterfield and Halliwell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: C. elegans has a short lifespan and a well-characterized nervous system.
source: C. elegans has a short lifespan, a well-characterized nervous system, and is therefore routinely used for studies in developmental biology, neurobiology, aging and mitochondrial biology (Gruber et al., 2015; Ghosh-Roy and Chisholm, 2010; Corsi, 2015; Dancy, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: Temperature-inducible C. elegans strains which express high levels of Aβ in muscle exhibit obvious Aβ aggregates, rapid paralysis and die within 2–3 days.
source: In particular, temperature-inducible strains which, upon induction, express high levels of Aβ in muscle, exhibit obvious Aβ aggregates, rapid paralysis and die within 2–3 days (Link, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on C. elegans AD models.

claim: C. elegans strains with comparatively low-level of neuronal Aβ expression do not produce obvious aggregates and typically display milder effects, such as a reduction in egg-laying, progressive chemotaxis defects, neuronal loss and a 10–20% lifespan reduction.
source: Strains with a comparatively low-level of neuronal Aβ expression do not produce obvious aggregates and typically display milder effects, such as a reduction in egg-laying, progressive chemotaxis defects, neuronal loss and a 10–20% lifespan reduction (Wu et al., 2006; Fong et al., 2016; Treusch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on C. elegans AD models.

claim: GRU102 displays comparatively mild phenotypes including failure in chemotaxis, with neuromuscular and behavioral defects that become more pronounced with age.
source: Similar to previous transgenic strains expressing Aβ in neurons, GRU102 display comparatively mild phenotypes including failure in chemotaxis, with neuromuscular and behavioral defects that become more pronounced with age.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic characterization of the GRU102 strain.

claim: Aβ aggregates were detectable only in old GRU102 (day 12).
source: Remarkably, even though Aβ aggregates were detectable only in old GRU102 (day 12), we found defects in energy metabolism and significantly reduced activity in mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) complexes in GRU102 already when young (Fong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: Defects in energy metabolism and significantly reduced activity in mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) complexes were found in GRU102 already when young.
source: Remarkably, even though Aβ aggregates were detectable only in old GRU102 (day 12), we found defects in energy metabolism and significantly reduced activity in mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) complexes in GRU102 already when young (Fong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors' previous publication.

claim: Antioxidant treatment using MitoQ ameliorated depletion of the mitochondrial lipid cardiolipin and improved healthspan of CL2006.
source: For instance, we have previously shown that antioxidant treatment, using the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant MitoQ, ameliorated depletion of the mitochondrial lipid cardiolipin and improved healthspan of another strain of transgenic AD nematodes with muscular expression of Aβ (CL2006) (Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Metformin treatment delayed Aβ-related paralysis and improved neuronal transmission in two transgenic AD strains, one with inducible muscular (CL4176) and one with neuronal Aβ expression (CL2355).
source: Treatment using an antidiabetic drug, Metformin, has also recently been shown to delay Aβ-related paralysis, and improve neuronal transmission, in two transgenic AD strains, one with inducible muscular (CL4176) and one with neuronal Aβ expression (CL2355) (Ahmad and Ebert, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Levels of the common energy precursor C2 (Acetylcarnitine) were significantly reduced in old GRU102 compared to age-matched GRU101 controls.
source: We found that levels of the common energy precursor C2 were significantly reduced in old GRU102 compared to age-matched GRU101 controls (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), reflecting a low energy status in old GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AA-derived AC species (C3-carnitine) was significantly reduced in old GRU102.
source: AA-derived AC species (C3-carnitine) was also significantly reduced in old GRU102 (Figure 1A), suggesting that AA metabolism was affected in old GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FA-derived AC species remained unchanged in old GRU102.
source: By contrast, FA-derived AC species remained unchanged (Figure 1A), suggesting that FA metabolism remained intact even in old GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Levels of storage lipids, Triacylglycerides (TAGs), between GRU102 and GRU101 remained similar.
source: These findings agree with the observation that levels of storage lipids, Triacylglycerides (TAGs), between GRU102 and GRU101 remained similar (Figure 1B) while lower total AA levels were observed in old GRU102 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lower total AA levels were observed in old GRU102.
source: These findings agree with the observation that levels of storage lipids, Triacylglycerides (TAGs), between GRU102 and GRU101 remained similar (Figure 1B) while lower total AA levels were observed in old GRU102 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of glucogenic AA forming alpha-Ketoglutarate (aKG) was significantly increased in old GRU102 animals compared to age-matched controls.
source: This analysis of the AA profile demonstrated that, in comparison to age-matched controls, the percentage of glucogenic AA forming forming alpha-Ketoglutarate (aKG) was significantly increased in old GRU102 animals (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both fumarate and malate were significantly reduced in old GRU102.
source: However, both of the TCA cycle intermediates, fumarate and malate, were significantly reduced in old GRU102 (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The FBA suggested a ~ 3 fold reduced production of cytosolic aKG from glutamate in GRU102 compared to GRU101.
source: Comparing the metabolic flux distributions between young GRU101 and GRU102, the FBA suggested a more than two-fold flux changes in several reactions related to aKG, including a ~ 3 fold reduced production of cytosolic aKG from glutamate and a ~ 10 fold increased production of cytosolic aKG from 3phosphohydroxypyruvate.
evidence: This is based on computational metabolic flux balance analysis.

claim: The FBA suggested a ~ 10 fold increased production of cytosolic aKG from 3phosphohydroxypyruvate in GRU102 compared to GRU101.
source: Comparing the metabolic flux distributions between young GRU101 and GRU102, the FBA suggested a more than two-fold flux changes in several reactions related to aKG, including a ~ 3 fold reduced production of cytosolic aKG from glutamate and a ~ 10 fold increased production of cytosolic aKG from 3phosphohydroxypyruvate.
evidence: This is based on computational metabolic flux balance analysis.

claim: The model predicted a reversal in the direction of flux in the alanine-pyruvate cycle between GRU101 and GRU102.
source: The model predicted a reversal in the direction of flux in the alanine-pyruvate cycle, where, in young GRU101, alanine and aKG are converted to pyruvate and glutamate, but in GRU102, pyruvate and glutamate are converted to alanine and aKG (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on computational metabolic flux balance analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: A significant reduction in aKGDH activity relative to age-matched GRU101 controls was observed in old but not young GRU102.
source: We observed a significant reduction in aKGDH activity relative to age-matched GRU101 controls in old but not young GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data.

claim: aKGDH knockdown significantly reduced both basal and maximal respiration in GRU101.
source: We found that aKGDH knockdown significantly reduced both basal and maximal respiration in GRU101, an effect similar to the defects in GRU102 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic flux data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The response to the addition of chemical uncoupler appeared both delayed and blunted in GRU101 with adult aKGDH knockdown, similar to GRU102.
source: Notably, as for GRU102, the response to the addition of chemical uncoupler appeared both delayed and blunted in GRU101 with adult aKGDH knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic flux data.

claim: Further loss of aKGDH did not significantly affect lifespan in GRU102.
source: To evaluate if loss of aKGDH might be a compensatory mechanism, we also carried out lifespan studies in GRU102 subject to RNAi knockdown of aKGDH but found that further loss of this enzyme did not significantly affect lifespan, suggesting that reduced aKGDH activity is not protective in GRU102 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of aKGDH significantly worsened the metabolic flux in GRU102 animals.
source: We also evaluated metabolic effects of aKGDH knockdown in GRU102 and found that loss of aKGDH similarly did not normalize but instead significantly worsened the metabolic flux in GRU102 animals (Figure 3C), further confirming that reduction in aKGDH is detrimental in AD.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic flux data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The OCR during uncoupling of GRU102 correlates well with that of GRU101 fed with aKGDH RNAi (r = 0.98, p<0.001).
source: We found that the OCR during uncoupling of GRU102 correlates well with that of GRU101 fed with aKGDH RNAi (r = 0.98, p<0.001) but not for animals fed EV (r = 0.33, p=ns, Figure 3D), illustrating that aKGDH knockdown causes GRU101 to experience deficits in the response to uncoupling that resembles GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of OCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both GRU102 and GRU101 subject to aKGDH knockdown suffer a significant delay in reaching maximal uncoupled respiration following addition of FCCP.
source: To directly quantify this effect, we compared the time needed for OCR values to rise to at least two standard deviation above the average coupled (basal) respiration, finding that, while GRU101 rapidly responded to addition of FCCP, both GRU102 and GRU101 subject to aKGDH knockdown suffer a significant delay (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of OCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: aKGDH has been reported to be sensitive to inactivation by reactive oxygen species (ROS), in part through the oxidation of lipoic acid bound covalently to the E2 subunit of aKGDH.
source: aKGDH has been reported to be sensitive to inactivation by reactive oxygen species (ROS), in part through the oxidation of lipoic acid bound covalently to the E2 subunit of aKGDH (Tretter and Adam-Vizi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ has been reported to directly promote oxidative stress.
source: Oxidative stress is thought to contribute to the pathophysiology of AD (Swomley and Butterfield, 2015; Tramutola et al., 2017) and Aβ has been reported to directly promote oxidative stress (Mattson and Mattson, 2002; Huang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Total PCC in whole body worm lysate was unchanged in GRU102.
source: While total PCC in whole body worm lysate was unchanged in GRU102 (Figure 4A), we found a significant elevation in mitochondrial protein carbonyls (mtPCC) even in young GRU102 when compared to GRU101 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by protein carbonyl assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A significant elevation in mitochondrial protein carbonyls (mtPCC) was found even in young GRU102 when compared to GRU101.
source: While total PCC in whole body worm lysate was unchanged in GRU102 (Figure 4A), we found a significant elevation in mitochondrial protein carbonyls (mtPCC) even in young GRU102 when compared to GRU101 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by protein carbonyl assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Metformin at a dose of 50 mM rescued the lifespan deficit of GRU102 by normalizing its median lifespan to that of untreated GRU101.
source: We found that Metformin at a dose of 50 mM rescued the lifespan deficit of GRU102 by normalizing its median lifespan to that of untreated GRU101 (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Metformin treatment reduced the percentage of dead GRU102 following challenge with Paraquat.
source: Metformin treatment also strengthened stress defense of GRU102, as seen in the reduced in percentage of dead GRU102 following challenge with Paraquat (Figure 5B), a herbicide that induces superoxide production (Wiemer and Osiewacz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by Paraquat stress resistance data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Metformin treatment significantly increased maximal respiratory capacity of GRU102 to a level that was still lower than that of untreated GRU101.
source: While old GRU102 exhibited significantly impaired respiratory capacity, Metformin treatment significantly increased maximal respiratory capacity of GRU102 to a level that was, however, still lower than that of untreated GRU101 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic flux data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Metformin treatment increased the abundance of many AA in GRU102, with Alanine, Glycine, Proline and Serine consistently increased in both replicates.
source: We found that Metformin treatment increased the abundance of many AA in GRU102, with Alanine, Glycine, Proline and Serine consistently increased in both replicates (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Metformin treatment significantly reduced the level of fat-derived C18:1-carnitine in GRU102.
source: Interestingly, at the same time that it increased AA related metabolites, Metformin treatment significantly reduced the level of fat-derived C18:1-carnitine (Figure 5E), suggesting that Metformin reduced the amount of energy derived from lipid metabolism relative to that derived from AA metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Metformin treatment reduced the level of lactate in GRU102 while at the same time increasing the levels of pyruvate, fumarate and malate.
source: Metformin treatment also reduced the level of lactate in GRU102 while at the same time increasing the levels of pyruvate, fumarate and malate.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Levels of malate in Metformin-treated GRU102 were significantly higher than those in GRU101.
source: Levels of malate were in fact significantly higher than those in GRU101 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A previous proteomic analysis of Metformin-treated WT C. elegans suggested an enrichment of proteins involved in branched-chain amino acid degradation and TCA cycle metabolism.
source: Our metabolomics findings were consistent with a previous proteomic analysis of Metformin-treated WT C. elegans, which suggested an enrichment of proteins involved in branched-chain amino acid degradation and TCA cycle metabolism (De Haes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Metformin reverted the levels of Pyruvate, Histidine, Alanine and Glutamine in old GRU102 back to that of the young GRU102.
source: Interestingly, Metformin treatment reverted the levels of these metabolites (Pyruvate, Histidine, Alanine and Glutamine) in old GRU102 back to that of the young GRU102 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that Metformin reverses the aging-related metabolic decline of metabolites in cluster 1.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Sulfomethoxazole (SMX) has been shown to extend lifespan in nematodes, establishing a link between folate inhibition and lifespan extension.
source: Sulfomethoxazole (SMX), a sulfonamide antibiotics that blocks folate synthesis, has similarly been shown to extend lifespan in nematodes, establishing a link between folate inhibition and lifespan extension (Virk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: SMX did not rescue the metabolic flux impairment or the lifespan detriment of GRU102.
source: We found that SMX did not rescue the metabolic flux impairment or the lifespan detriment of GRU102 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The beneficial effects of Metformin in GRU102 were unlikely to be mediated predominantly by inhibition of microbiome folate production.
source: These observations suggest that the beneficial effects of Metformin in GRU102 were unlikely to be mediated predominantly by inhibition of microbiome folate production.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of SMX on GRU102 phenotypes.

claim: When the animals were young, no difference in the levels of insoluble protein was detected between GRU102 and GRU101.
source: Using this normalization we found that, when the animals were young, no difference in the levels of insoluble protein was detected between GRU102 and GRU101 (Figure 6C), indicating that the proteostasis machinery of young GRU102 is still relatively intact.
evidence: This is supported by protein aggregation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Aged GRU102 displayed significantly higher levels of insoluble protein compared to age-matched GRU101.
source: However, aged GRU102 displayed significantly higher levels of insoluble protein compared to age-matched GRU101 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by protein aggregation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The levels of protein aggregates in the Metformin-treated GRU102 appear similar to the GRU101 and the difference between GRU101 and Metformin-treated GRU102 was no longer statistically significant.
source: However, we also observed that the levels of protein aggregates in the Metformin-treated GRU102 appear similar to the GRU101 and the difference between GRU101 and Metformin-treated GRU102 was no longer statistically significant (Figure 6C, One-way ANOVA multiple comparisons test p=ns).
evidence: This is supported by protein aggregation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Energy deficits and reduced activities of mitochondrial ETC complexes are early events in GRU102, well before any detectable Aβ aggregates are present.
source: We have previously reported that energy deficits and reduced activities of mitochondrial ETC complexes are early events in GRU102, well before any detectable Aβ aggregates are present (Fong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Key energy substrates, in particular glucogenic AA that form pyruvate and aKG, as well as the TCA cycle intermediates fumarate and malate, are selectively affected in GRU102.
source: Here, we have shown that key energy substrates, in particular glucogenic AA that form pyruvate and aKG, as well as the TCA cycle intermediates fumarate and malate, are selectively affected in GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: aKGDH is a rate-limiting enzyme in the TCA cycle.
source: Given that aKGDH is a rate-limiting enzyme in the TCA cycle (Huang et al., 2003), reduced aKGDH activity is a plausible explanation for reduced flux through the TCA cycle, ATP production and maximum respiratory capacity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Reduced aKGDH activity is a plausible explanation for reduced flux through the TCA cycle, ATP production and maximum respiratory capacity in GRU102.
source: Given that aKGDH is a rate-limiting enzyme in the TCA cycle (Huang et al., 2003), reduced aKGDH activity is a plausible explanation for reduced flux through the TCA cycle, ATP production and maximum respiratory capacity.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of aKGDH and the observed defects in GRU102.

claim: Reduction in aKGDH activity is detrimental to metabolic capacity in adults.
source: These results suggest that reduction in aKGDH activity is detrimental to metabolic capacity in adults and that it alone can recapitulate the metabolic deficits of AD in C. elegans.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Inactivation of specific enzymes involved in the TCA may be a key mechanism of Aβ toxicity.
source: This, of course, does not mean that inactivation of aKGDH is the single cause of the metabolic detriments in Aβ1–42-expressing C. elegans, but it suggests that inactivation of specific enzymes involved in the TCA may be a key mechanism of Aβ toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results on aKGDH.

claim: Mitochondrial-specific ROS is a potential early cause of mitochondrial dysfunction in GRU102.
source: Our study revealed mitochondrial-specific ROS as a potential early cause of mitochondrial dysfunction in our AD model, as shown by the early (day 4) increase in mtPCC but not in global PCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed increase in mtPCC but not global PCC.

claim: The mitochondrial enzyme aKGDH is particularly sensitive to inactivation by ROS (hydrogen peroxide) in vitro.
source: In vitro experiments have shown that the mitochondrial enzyme aKGDH is particularly sensitive to inactivation by ROS (hydrogen peroxide) (Tretter and Adam-Vizi, 2000), consistent with the involvement of this enzyme in GRU102 metabolic defects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Site-specific oxidative modification to mitochondrial but not global protein is one possible mechanism to explain the reduction of aKGDH activity observed in old GRU102.
source: Site-specific oxidative modification to mitochondrial but not global protein is one possible mechanism to explain the reduction of aKGDH activity observed in old GRU102.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observed patterns of protein carbonylation and enzyme activity.

claim: Mitochondrial enzymes involved in energy regulation are known to be redox sensitive and often downregulated in AD.
source: These findings are consistent with other reports showing that mitochondrial enzymes involved in energy regulation are known to be redox sensitive and often downregulated in AD (Butterfield and Halliwell, 2019; Mastrogiacomo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metabolic deficits and increased mtPCC were detectable in young GRU102, while increased global protein aggregation was only seen in aged GRU102.
source: Remarkably, we found that metabolic deficits and increased mtPCC were detectable in young GRU102, while increased global protein aggregation was only seen in aged GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis of multiple assays in the manuscript.

claim: Impairment of proteostasis may be late or secondary to metabolic dysfunction and/or to oxidative inactivation of TCA cycle enzymes.
source: This sequence of events suggests that impairment of proteostasis may be late or secondary to metabolic dysfunction and/or to oxidative inactivation of TCA cycle enzymes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal sequence of events observed in the study.

claim: The Aβ-induced oxidative stress hypothesis of AD supports oxidative stress as a direct and cell-autonomous mechanism of Aβ-induced toxicity.
source: While our data currently do not address this question, the Aβ-induced oxidative stress hypothesis of AD (see Introduction paragraph 2) supports oxidative stress as a direct and cell-autonomous mechanism of Aβ-induced toxicity (Butterfield and Halliwell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: ROS-mediated elevation in PCC are only observed in brain regions of AD subjects rich in Aβ-plaques, but not in other brain regions devoid of Aβ-plaques.
source: The confined effects of oxidative stress in Aβ-expressing neurons is also supported by clinical findings that ROS-mediated elevation in PCC are only observed in brain regions of AD subjects rich in Aβ-plaques, but not in other brain regions devoid of Aβ-plaques (Hensley et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical findings.

claim: Activation of stress response mechanism and proteotoxicity are non-cell-autonomous consequences in protein-misfolding diseases including AD.
source: On the other hand, existing literature has suggested the activation of stress response mechanism and proteotoxicity as non-cell-autonomous consequences in protein-misfolding diseases including AD (Nussbaum-Krammer and Morimoto, 2014), as activation of stress response, such as the heat shock response or unfolded protein response, functions at a whole animal level, beyond the immediate affected cell (Nussbaum-Krammer and Morimoto, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Induction of mitochondrial stress in neurons can lead to non-cell-autonomous mitochondrial stress response in non-neuronal compartment such as intestine in C. elegans.
source: Studies in C. elegans have also shown that induction of mitochondrial stress in neurons can lead to non-cell-autonomous mitochondrial stress response in non-neuronal compartment such as intestine (Durieux et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Metformin has previously been shown to strengthen stress defense, and to increase branched-chain AA degradation and TCA metabolism in WT C. elegans.
source: Metformin has previously been shown to strengthen stress defense, and to increase branched-chain AA degradation and TCA metabolism in WT C. elegans (De Haes et al., 2014; Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metformin treatment normalizes lifespan and mitochondrial function in GRU102 up to the level of untreated GRU101 controls.
source: We found that Metformin treatment normalizes lifespan and mitochondrial function in GRU102 up to the level of untreated GRU101 controls.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan and metabolic flux data in the manuscript.

claim: Lifespan of the Metformin-treated GRU102 was even longer than the untreated GRU101.
source: Lifespan of the Metformin-treated GRU102 was even longer than the untreated GRU101.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data in the manuscript.

claim: Metformin treatment restores respiratory capacity and improves the availability of glucogenic AA and TCA cycle intermediates in the GRU102 animals.
source: Consistent with previous studies showing that Metformin improves AA and TCA cycle metabolism in WT C. elegans (De Haes et al., 2014), we demonstrated that Metformin treatment also restores respiratory capacity and improves the availability of glucogenic AA and TCA cycle intermediates in the GRU102 animals.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics and metabolic flux data in the manuscript.

claim: Metabolic health and proteostasis are closely related to each other.
source: While more work needs to be carried out to confirm the causal relationship between metabolic dysfunction and protein aggregation, our observation is consistent with findings that metabolic health and proteostasis are closely related to each other (Ruan et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017; Fang et al., 2019; Guerrero-Gómez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metformin can penetrate through the blood brain barrier.
source: Given that Metformin can penetrate through the blood brain barrier (Ying et al., 2015), our findings suggest Metformin as an alternative therapy for AD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Clinical trials of Metformin in MCI and mild AD patients have suggested improvement in cognitive function in the Metformin-treated groups.
source: Clinical trials of Metformin in MCI and mild AD patients have also suggested improvement in cognitive function in the Metformin-treated groups (Koenig et al., 2017; Luchsinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trials.

claim: The dose of Metformin used in this study (50 mM, equivalent to 8.25 g/L) is approximately five times higher than the therapeutic concentrations of plasma Metformin reported in humans (up to 1.8 g/L).
source: However, we noted that the dose of Metformin used in this study (50 mM, equivalent to 8.25 g/L) is approximately five times higher than the therapeutic concentrations of plasma Metformin reported in humans (up to 1.8 g/L) (Kajbaf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental dose with reported human therapeutic concentrations.

claim: The low permeability of C. elegans cuticle to exogenous drug compounds often leads to the much higher drug concentration needed for therapeutic effects.
source: This difference could be due to the low permeability of C. elegans cuticle to exogenous drug compounds, which often leads to the much higher drug concentration needed for therapeutic effects (Chisholm and Xu, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on C. elegans drug delivery.

claim: Metabolic failure is an early and central event in AD pathogenesis.
source: In conclusion, our results suggest metabolic failure as an early and central event in AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data in the study.

claim: Metabolic interventions that normalize metabolic dysfunction may be beneficial to prevent or reduce AD pathogenesis.
source: Metabolic interventions that normalize metabolic dysfunction may therefore be beneficial to prevent or reduce AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the beneficial effects of Metformin observed in the study.

claim: GRU102 expresses human Aβ1-42 under the unc-119 promoter.
source: The transgenic strains, GRU101[myo-2p::yfp] and GRU102[myo-2p::yfp + unc-119p::Aβ1–42], previously reported in Fong et al. (2016) were used in all experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the strains used.

claim: GRU101 is a transgenic control strain that does not express Aβ.
source: The transgenic strains, GRU101[myo-2p::yfp] and GRU102[myo-2p::yfp + unc-119p::Aβ1–42], previously reported in Fong et al. (2016) were used in all experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the strain description showing GRU101 lacks the Aβ transgene present in GRU102.

claim: Young animals in this study refer to day 4 post-bleaching.
source: Young animals refer to day four post-bleaching while old animals refer to day 12 post-bleaching.
evidence: This is explicitly defined in the methods section.

claim: Old animals in this study refer to day 12 post-bleaching.
source: Young animals refer to day four post-bleaching while old animals refer to day 12 post-bleaching.
evidence: This is explicitly defined in the methods section.

claim: Acylcarnitines (AC) are intermediates that are typically generated during the transport of activated long-chain fatty acids (FA) from the cytosol to mitochondria for FA oxidation.
source: AC are intermediates that are typically generated during the transport of activated long-chain fatty acids (FA) from the cytosol to mitochondria for FA oxidation (Schooneman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Propionylcarnitine (C3) and Isovalerylcarnitine (C5) are derived from the degradation of branched-chain AA.
source: For example, Propionylcarnitine (C3) and Isovalerylcarnitine (C5) are derived from the degradation of branched-chain AA while Acetylcarnitine (C2) is a common energy precursor derived from glucose and FA metabolism (Schooneman et al., 2013; Rinaldo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Acetylcarnitine (C2) is a common energy precursor derived from glucose and FA metabolism.
source: For example, Propionylcarnitine (C3) and Isovalerylcarnitine (C5) are derived from the degradation of branched-chain AA while Acetylcarnitine (C2) is a common energy precursor derived from glucose and FA metabolism (Schooneman et al., 2013; Rinaldo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: AA can be metabolized to produce energy via glucogenic pathways where they are converted into pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate (aKG), succinyl CoA, fumarate or oxaloacetate, which can then participate in the TCA cycle.
source: AA can be metabolized to produce energy via glucogenic pathways where they are converted into pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate (aKG), succinyl CoA, fumarate or oxaloacetate, which can then participate in the TCA cycle (Hayamizu, 2017).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Protein carbonylation is a consequence of oxidative damage to protein.
source: Protein carbonylation is a consequence of oxidative damage to protein and protein carbonyl content (PCC) is routinely used to assess ROS-related protein oxidation (Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Protein carbonyl content (PCC) is routinely used to assess ROS-related protein oxidation.
source: Protein carbonylation is a consequence of oxidative damage to protein and protein carbonyl content (PCC) is routinely used to assess ROS-related protein oxidation (Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Paraquat is a herbicide that induces superoxide production.
source: Metformin treatment also strengthened stress defense of GRU102, as seen in the reduced in percentage of dead GRU102 following challenge with Paraquat (Figure 5B), a herbicide that induces superoxide production (Wiemer and Osiewacz, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Paraquat supported by citation.

claim: Proteostasis is energetically expensive, because protein degradation, synthesis and quality control, required for turnover of misfolded proteins, are all energy-intensive processes.
source: Proteostasis is energetically expensive, because protein degradation, synthesis and quality control, required for turnover of misfolded proteins, are all energy-intensive processes (Hartl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Increased oxidative stress can disrupt protein homeostasis (proteostasis) through irreversible oxidation and subsequent modifications of proteins.
source: Increased oxidative stress can disrupt protein homeostasis (proteostasis) through irreversible oxidation and subsequent modifications of proteins, and such damage also impairs protein degradation (Squier, 2001).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Oxidative damage impairs protein degradation.
source: Increased oxidative stress can disrupt protein homeostasis (proteostasis) through irreversible oxidation and subsequent modifications of proteins, and such damage also impairs protein degradation (Squier, 2001).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Disruption in mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis can induce protein aggregation.
source: Our results, taken together with other recent findings, suggest that disruption in mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis can induce protein aggregation, and targeting these processes can be beneficial in AD (Ruan et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017; Fang et al., 2019; Guerrero-Gómez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the study results and supported by citations to related research.

claim: Targeting mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis can be beneficial in AD.
source: Our results, taken together with other recent findings, suggest that disruption in mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis can induce protein aggregation, and targeting these processes can be beneficial in AD (Ruan et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017; Fang et al., 2019; Guerrero-Gómez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the study results and supported by citations to related research.

claim: Metformin has been shown previously to improve stress resistance and increase TCA cycle metabolism in Wildtype (WT) C. elegans.
source: Given evidence for early disruption in energy metabolism and ROS-mediated damage in GRU102, we next examined whether Metformin, an anti-diabetic drug and metabolic modulator that has been shown previously to improve stress resistance and increase TCA cycle metabolism in Wildtype (WT) C. elegans (De Haes et al., 2014; Onken and Driscoll, 2010), was able to rescue Aβ-induced pathology in GRU102.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metformin has been previously shown to impact lifespan in C. elegans through inhibition of folate production by the microbiome.
source: Metformin has been previously shown to impact lifespan in C. elegans through inhibition of folate production by the microbiome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Succinyl CoA Synthetase (SCS) is an important regulator of mitochondrial integrity including in neurons.
source: Among those downstream enzymes, Succinyl CoA Synthetase (SCS) is an important regulator of mitochondrial integrity including in neurons (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Increased levels of Malate Dehydrogenase (MDH) have previously been found in the brain of AD patients.
source: Increased levels of another downstream enzyme, Malate Dehydrogenase (MDH), have previously been found in the brain of AD patients (Paterson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The pan-neuronal unc-119 promoter used to drive Aβ expression in GRU102 has been suggested to have low expression in intestine.
source: The pan-neuronal unc-119 promoter that we use to drive Aβ expression in GRU102 has been suggested to have low expression in intestine, and such expression might lead to detriments in that compartment not confined in the neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration for interpreting the results.
